chunks: Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shazan, and Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father, all from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hariz, from Zurara, who said:

I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), 'Does a man pray the night and day prayers all of them with one ablution?' He said, 'Yes, as long as he does not incur a breakage.' I said, 'And does he pray with one tayammum the night and day prayers all of them?' He said, 'Yes, as long as he does not incur a breakage or find water.' I said, 'If he finds water and hopes that he will be able to find another water, and thinks that he will be able to find it whenever he wishes, but that is difficult for him?' He said, 'That breaks his tayammum, and upon him is to repeat the tayammum.' I said, 'If he finds water and has already entered into the prayer?' He said, 'So let him turn away and let him perform ablution as long as he has not bowed; if he has bowed, let him continue in his prayer, for the tayammum is one of the two purifiers.'

key_terms.الطَّهُورَيْنِ: The two purifiers (referring to water and earth/dust)

ai.seo_question: What are the rules for continuing prayer with one wudu or tayammum if water is found?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the flexibility of ritual purity in Shia jurisprudence, affirming that a single wudu or tayammum suffices for all prayers until a nullifying event occurs, reflecting the principle of continuity (istishab). It provides precise legal rulings for scenarios where water is discovered during prayer, distinguishing between pre-ruku' and post-ruku' states to determine whether to restart or complete the prayer. This underscores the theological view that tayammum is a complete, independent purifier ('one of the two purifiers') rather than merely a temporary substitute.
